Kheng T
Dear Diner,
Thank you for your review comments on the quality of our meals and service. First we are not geared to tourists but service our loyal local diners that demand our authentic quality and hygiene safety. 
As you have noted, our prices are higher than other vendors who use the cheapest ingredients (in some cases synthetic meats) in order to attain the cheapest price. This action only assures a cheap price and a mediocre tasting product. In this instance, we differ from others as we consider quality and authenticity must always come first. 
OUR MANTRA WE LIVE BY: QUALITY IS A MUST: 
YOU ONLY GET WHAT YOU PAY FOR. First rate ingredients are critical in order to achieve the authentic tastes and quality of traditional Vietnamese dishes. It is important our customers know that we love what we do and are very proud of the authentic quality meals we are able to serve. MBM prepares meals blending only the finest authentic spices (no cheap artificial substitutes) with our Fresh Can Gio Jumbo Prawns and our imported Meats: USDA Choice Beef Steak (United States), Lean Beef Stew (Australia), Pork Shoulder from South America and Europe. Free-range Chicken and specialty greens are sourced from Dalat and highland farms, all accompanied with their provenance ensuring consistent quality, at a still reasonable price. MBM warrants that no better value may be found in the country for a quick gourmet meal, which is why we have served more than 2 million meals.
Our meals may cost a little more than elsewhere, but after spending a significant amount to arrange a visit to Vietnam…. Is spending a extra dollar worth ensuring that you are dining on a authentic tasting Vietnamese meal of quality and assures you of being a hygienically safe meal? We appreciate that only you can make personal value choices for yourself individually and thank you for dining with us and wishing you safe dining during your visit.

Healthy vs famous Michelin rated food
Jul 2026 • Family
Was pretty upset with the chicken banh mi that I was served with which has way too much char or black and burnt part from the chicken meat. I have never have so much char that I need to remove them before thinking of putting it into my mouth. For those who are health conscious traveller, its not worth risk your health to eat this restaurant rated 'michelin' which not preparing healthy food.
Read more
Written July 9, 2026
Kheng T
Dear Diner, 
If your health-conscious concerns are to charcoal grilling carcinogenic’ s, you first need to understand where your real concern with carcinogens should lie. The primary concern should not be with charcoal itself, but with high heat cooking and the item being grilled. Meats with high fat content are of the most concern… so whether you eat a steak grilled in a hot pan or over charcoal, carcinogen’s will, and do play a role in both. By the way…Chicken is very low in fat.
My question to you is: If you are concerned with charcoal grilling and carcinogen’s? Why did you order “charcoal grilled chicken.” If you wanted chicken, why did you not order our pan roasted version of chicken instead???
Your charcoal grilling fear would make for a very rainy day on the 4th of July in America… 
Understanding your dietary concern, I think it best you stick to a steamed diet….and wishing you a pleasant stay during your visit to Vietnam.

Dear Diner,
We assume when entering our restaurant and a quick review of our premises and menu, you undoubtedly noted we are an informal “Fine Dining” Vietnamese Bistro. We are not a common sidewalk food stall as you may have become used to. Also, we are somewhat surprised with your comment of “I couldn't believe the bill,” …. As you ordered from a menu where meal prices are clearly marked, we do not understand your comment. 
One must realize quality cost more and our being an informal fine dining establishment, we construct our meals with the finest quality ingredients. In this instance, it is worthy to note we airfreight and import chilled USDA Choice Beef from the US, Pork Shoulder from Brazil and Europe and serve Free Range Chicken. These ingredients cost us more, but this is the only way we know how to deliver the quality and taste we are famed for and our loyal diner’s demand. 
We trust you understand fine dining costs a little more even when served in an informal atmosphere. Wishing you a pleasant stay in Vietnam.

Truly hyped up and no value restaurant.

Dear Descus!
Thank you for your compliment on our dining ambiance and your making time to craft your review. Your efforts are greatly appreciated.
We do understand that your being a visitor to Vietnam, you may not be familiar with what an authentic meal should taste like.
For instance with respect to the Banh MI, the authentic Banh Mi introduced to 19th Century Saigon by the French was not the pickle, chili sauce sandwich that is served at the local sidewalk Banh Mi stand today. The French creators of the Banh Mi constructed their sandwiches with quality beef and pork to be their main ingredients.
The French creators of the Banh Mi chose the taste quality of their ingredients to be the main attraction of their Vietnamese sandwich introduction. This Banh Mi as a result of the quality was considered expensive and subsequently consumed primarily by the affluent.
Street stall operators recognizing the term “Banh Mi” as a status symbol decided to replicate a less expensive version using lower quality composite meats to cut costs. The cost cutting meat composites offered no taste after emulsification compression and subsequently, chili sauce and pickles were added to create a flavor and mask unwanted odors. 
You will note that our Beef is imported from the United States and flown chilled to Vietnam. Once received, we flame grill our USDA Choice Hanger Steak “Saignant” over flaming charcoal. This flame grilling is to sear in all the natural flavors of the quality USDA beef. 
As your review is in French, please try and imagine ordering a steak at a noted French restaurant and asking for Chili Sauce and Pickles for flavor?
One of the most important factors with the cheaper composite meats is hygiene….. If you search on Google, you will note that very recently as many as 400 diners were hospitalized in a week’s time suffering from composite meat food poisoning attributed to Banh Mis.
Whatever the case, we are a restaurant not a sidewalk stall that is noted for quality and authenticity serving the #1 Banh Mi in Vietnam. We do not compete on price but we do vigorously compete in serving meal quality, unparalleled hygiene offering great value for money. 
Thank you for dining with us and wishing you a memorable stay in Vietnam.

The important thing to understand is that the word “Banh Mi” does not indicate or identify a specific type of product… it simply means “Bread” and in Vietnam is commonly used to refer to a sandwich… Any Sandwich!!

As you can appreciate there is a distinct difference between a peanut butter and jelly sandwich and a “French Dip”, this also applies and distinguishes the difference between our Authentic Banh Mi (Colonial Anglo French Vietnamese) sandwich to that the current street sandwich. We are not criticizing the street sandwich, just noting that there is a distinct difference.

We replicate and serve the Banh Mi that was originally introduce to 19th Century Saigon by the French Culinary masters of the time. This is why we construct our Banh Mis with the highest quality fillings available as opposed to the composite type mystery meat fillings used by many a sidewalk vendor. 

The fact that our beef Banh Mi is constructed with slices of a slow roasted imported USDA Choice Hanger Steak makes a difference in both taste and cost. Whether you choose our beef, chicken, pork, fish Bo Kho, or Thit Kho belly pork Banh Mi, all are constructed with the highest quality ingredients and layered on our own specially baked dense baguette. 

We hope this satisfactorily explains why the quality and authenticity of our Banh Mis cost a little more.

Thank you again for your review and we hope to have the opportunity to serve you once again.

I have been living in HCM City for many years and I have sampled and enjoyed many fine restaurants, cafe's and eatery's around the city.

There is one in particular place that my wife and I, return to, over and over again. It's called "My Banh Mi". It's located just off of Don Koi St. within eye shot of the Norte Dame Cathedral and the Central Post Office.

It's an intimate and well established restaurant. It feels casual, unobtrusive and relaxed and that's far from all it's magic charms. 
 
Don't let its compact, hideaway, nature and ambiance fool you. From the minute you cross the threshold, until your ready to exit the premises. You'll be met by a high standard of professional courtesy, kindness - respect and prompt service. The kind you'd expect by a well trained bi - lingual staff. 

"My Banh Mi", has a family friendly flair that ads a special dimension to the time you spend there. The classic 60's and 70's era music that seems to be forever present in the back ground, ads a cool, quasi, Art Deco element to the mix. 
On one of the sidewalls, literally hundreds upon hundreds of foreign patrons, have commented about their experience at "My Banh Mi". Everyone, expressing their own version of a similarly shared feeling. 

Their enjoyment, good fortune / appreciation for the place, 
coming forth in a myriad of written ways, like a chronicle of kudos, laced by positive reflections that never seem to falter or end.

Some of the noteworthy specifics that are simply the way it is at "My Banh Mi", is as follows. The service is always stellar, the decor simple, but immensely, welcoming and you can count on the place being well lit, highlighting a clean - orderly appearance. 
 
However, it's crown jewel so to speak, is the uncanny ability of the management to consistently offer, a heightened level of quality and enviable, food freshness. Which is to die for and in my humble opinion, puts this bistro a cut above and beyond the norm. 

To top it all off, the crew maintains an enlightened focus which translates to a routine manner, by which all their Entree's are meticulously prepared, expertly presented and served with care. 
It's that international - professional energy which essentially, enables the place to stand out as one of the best finds in Saigon. 
Frank Chinn, the manager is a Chinese American, Ex Pat, who has been living in Saigon for about 25 years. He is an older gent, who has a good heart and all inclusive, engaging, presence, which will disarm and endear even the most guarded tourist. 
He is what he is, a bit a charmer, a bit of cad and always entertaining, while of course, never dropping the ball in making sure everyone of his guests gets what they want and enjoys what they get (without question).

To be perfectly clear and blunt, my favorite attribute and the main reason this somewhat obscure, sweet spot, has been held in high esteem, by Lyly and I. I definitely would refer this joint to anyone who appreciates and enjoys the benefits of being and experiencing a genuine, class act with a long standing, well established reputation.

Best to all, Philip and Ly

Kheng T
Dear missypinkaholic,

Thank you for your review comments. We do understand that our Banh Mis can and will taste different to those purchased from a street stall. First, one must understand that there is a very distinct difference between an authentic and original Banh Mi compared to that of the street cart Banh Mi. As such, please allow us to explain the reason for the difference. 

READ ON ONLY IF INTERESTED IN THE DIFFERENCE 

Our restaurant serves an authentic Banh Mi that is constructed to exactingly mirror the Banh Mi sandwich that was introduced to 19th Century Saigon by the French. Simply confirming such one only needs look at the basic ingredients. The baguette is French and the introduction of Pate was also French. The sandwich fillings used by the French in their original Banh Mi was a quality roasted beef, chicken or pork. The only difference between the Banh Mi introduced to Saigon and a sandwich in France was the garnish. Instead of using lettuce and tomato, the French fused local greens constructing their Banh Mi with cilantro, cucumber and mild chilies. (This was probably the first 19th Century dining fusion).

The original Banh Mi was expensive as a result of the quality ingredients required. This sandwich was only consumed by the affluent as it was too costly for the masses. As such, the Banh Mi attained somewhat of a celebrity status just as branded garments and accessories have achieved in current day.

As there was and continues to remain until today, a calling for cheap food in the streets, creative Vietnamese street vendors understood that the Vietnamese word “Banh Mi” simply meant “Bread.” As such, the street vendor could capitalize on the Banh Mi brand recognition by taking any bread product resembling a baguette, inserting any type of filling and thus could rightfully and correctly call their bread product a Banh Mi! 

The broad term “Banh Mi” allowed the street vendor to use any filling they wanted, on any bread product that resembled a baguette shape and could accurately call their product a Banh Mi.

As the street Banh Mi is constructed primarily with cost in mind, cheaper lower quality ingredients are used in their construction. If you notice that the baguette of street Banh Mi is light and appears hollow, there is a reason. To cut costs, the bread dough is infused with a chemical that cause the bread to puff up and basically remains hollow and primarily creating only an exterior outside crust. If you weighed a street banh mi baguette, you would find that it weighs one third of what our authentic French baguettes weigh. If you looked at the street sandwich filling, you will note that they primarily fill their baguette with a composite meat that had been emulsified, dyed and compressed from an animal product of unknown origin.

Street Banh Mis have a place and they fill the need for street diners on a limited budget to secure a cheap meal to fill an empty stomach. You may also note that the street banh mi is generously doused with a large portion of pickles and chili sauce. This serves the purpose of creating a flavor and also masking any unwanted odors.

We will not delve into the many differences between our Banh Mi and a street Banh Mi i.e. hygiene, potential contamination, etc. We trust our explanation allows you to now appreciate why we allow our quality Beef (Imported USDA Choice NY Strip Loin), Chicken, Pork and other authentic Vietnamese fillings to rightfully represent their inherent taste and flavors in the authentic Banh Mis we specialize in serving. (We do not require chili sauce or pickles to create flavor).

It is worthy to note that numerous professional food reviewers have rated us as serving the #1 Banh Mi in Vietnam for taste authenticity and quality. This opinion of authenticity and quality is also confirmed by the thousands upon thousands of local and visiting patrons we have appreciatively served over the years.

We thank you for your review and we do hope for the opportunity in future to serve you once again.

You many ask what the difference may be between what was originally introduced by the French as opposed to what is being sold on the streets today. The answer is very simple; the original Banh Mi was a high-end meal product requiring quality ingredients. Subsequently, once the Banh Mi was introduced the masses of budget oriented street diners could not afford the original Banh Mi quality. As such, a street product was developed to be sold at street carts at very cheap price for street diners. As a result of the cost cutting of ingredients, quality had to be seriously sacrificed. 

This degradation of ingredients resulted in quality being omitted with flavor being substituted with pickled vegetables and chili sauce. Also, the pickled vegetables and chili sauce garnishing served two purposes, it provided flavor to the flavorless composite lunch meat product being used and it masked a number of unwanted odors.

You mention our Banh Mi being somewhat fusion in taste and construction…one must remember the Banh Mi is probably one of the first culinary fusion dishes created. It was a French baguette, a French style Pate, a French style quality roasted meat and then simply garnished with local Vietnamese greens of cilantro, cucumber, julienned chili rather than the traditional French lettuce and tomato.

As a result of price, immigrating Vietnamese settling in new homelands replicated the cheap street version of the Banh Mi as this is what they knew. In actuality, this is no different to the global franchising of the fast food version of the Hamburger, Pizza or Taco. 

We trust our explanation has cast light on what the difference is between our authentic quality Banh Mi and that of a street Banh Mi sandwich. The simple difference between the two is all about quality and taste.

Dear Dev J,

Thank you for your review stating “Cheap, safe (i.e. non street food) eating option. Fresh and tasty.”

In actuality, we serve the original authentic Vietnamese meals that street vendors attempt to replicate with lower priced substitute ingredients. The lowering of quality is desired by street vendors to accommodate street diners on tight budgets and unconcerned with taste authenticity, quality or hygiene. 

Basically, in Vietnam there are two types of meals. The authentic meals that one can try in notable restaurants and the other being cheaper meals items that are constructed on and for the streets. 

The difference is that the authentic meal is prepared with quality ingredients and authentic spices. As a result of the ingredients and spices being of quality and authenticity, the authentic Vietnamese meal costs more than street food. 

As a result of relatively lax food and dining regulations, street food hygiene and quality is not akin to that demanded by a franchised fast food burger or taco vendor in the west. 

If you have eaten on the street, you will have noted that the majority of street foods employ an abundance of chilies or chemical chili sauce, pickled vegetables and/or fish sauce to dominate their food item. This is to create flavor or mask unwanted odors from lower quality composite meats or other substitute items being used. 

The biggest concern with street food is the hygiene and lack of sanitation as the ingredients are not refrigerated and are openly exposed on the street. Local residents have developed somewhat of an immunity to the crawling, flying and airborne bacteria abounding in the streets. This is not to say that a visitor to Vietnam is guaranteed a stomach problem when dining on the street but it is a definite possibility. Better and safer to cross the street with your eyes open than when closed. 

We trust our explanation on the two different styles of food available in Vietnam is helpful. This should explain the difference in taste quality and price between that of street food and a meal being served in a restaurant.

Not a review reply… TripAdvisor readers education 

TripAdvisor readers beware - we have found that not all reviews are sincere or accurate. As one can understand, fraudulent reviews are almost impossible to document. As such, we simply provide facts and leave the decision on factuality to the readers.

As such, for the benefit of TripAdvisor readers, we are taking the time to explain and document the difference between the price of an authentic Banh Mi such as what we serve at My Banh Mi, as compared to that of street stalls vendors. 

Actually when explaining a price difference, the authenticity of taste, quality of ingredients, food hygiene practices and meal service…… are the supporting influences for price differences. As we all know, quality costs a little more but when it comes to food in an emerging market, price justifies the quality and most importantly, food hygiene and consumption safety. 

The fact is that the Banh Mi we serve is authentic and exactingly mirrors the taste authenticity and quality of the original Banh Mi introduced to 19th century Saigon by the French. Our focus is on quality and hygiene.

Also, one should remember that is was the French who originated and introduced the Banh Mi to Vietnam. The baguette is French and so is Pate. The original and authentic Banh Mi was never an inexpensive meal but was an example of a French/Vietnamese fusion of quality ingredients. The Banh Mi is a French fusion sandwich. 

Also, it is worthy to note that the word Banh Mi in Vietnamese simply means bread and later coined to mean a sandwich, ….any sandwich. As such, a sandwich from My Banh Mi cannot be compared to the lower quality reinvented street stall banh mi. The street stall take-away sandwich is different.

My Banh Mi is not a street stall; we are a sit down boutique type restaurant. As such, our meal quality, service, hygiene and ambiance are totally different to a take-away street stall. The reviewer attempts to compare our restaurant to a street stall but this is akin to attempting to compare apples with oranges. Both may be fruit but both are entirely different. As such, the simple use of bread does not make for an authentic Banh Mi. 

Fact is, street vendors specializing in cheaper “take away” sandwiches are forced to use lower quality ingredients to suffice street diners living on a tight budget.

As such, cost cutting by stall operators is primary to their existence. This results in street vendors cutting corners. For instance, the using of chemically infused dough to blow up dough when baked to create the appearance of volume. In actuality, this dough when baked expands and becomes distorted in size usually leaving nothing more than a large empty hollow crust. Try a street Banh Mi and look inside the bread…. It is empty and is primarily only a crust.

In addition, the cost cutting measures in the baking of the bread most street vendors require their sandwiches to be constructed with a quasi mystery type “look alike” lunch meat. This less expensive quasi lunch meat composite is derived from the emulsifying, dyeing and compression of unknown animals and their parts. Exactly what animal and what parts is always the question. 

Also, cost cutting is not limited to food items but also to ingredient storage. Refrigeration costs money and as such, street stall ingredients are openly exposed to flying, crawling insects and the countless strains of airborne bacteria that abound in emerging markets.

In comparison, as a restaurant, we at My Banh Mi offer air-conditioned sit- down dining, table service and the assurance of demanding hygiene practices being maintained. We also employ well trained English speaking wait staff who are capable of assisting patrons in ordering correctly to their individual taste (savory, spicy, sweet etc.). Also, the staff is capable of providing insightful Vietnamese authentic meal recommendations.

As such, we question this reviewer’s logic in their attempt to compare our imported US Beef and our quality oven roasted meats to that of a street stall? This is more than baffling.

Street stalls are necessary and have their place in sufficing budget oriented diners who are more concerned with price than taste or hygiene. Street stalls fulfill a very important necessity for those who are forced by price to be satisfied on downgraded quality. This is equal in a developed market to eating at a franchised fast food operator rather than a quality restaurant. Both suffice a need.

Enough written on the comparisons.

If you visit Google or TripAdvisor and search for the Best beef, pork, chicken, fish or vegetarian Banh Mis in Ho Chi Minh City, you will find that our name will appear as the #1 Banh Mi in all of these categories. 

Do not just check for a filling type such as Beef or Fish but specifically specify the Best before the filling and you will find that we dominate the #1 position in all categories.

The recognition we receive for authenticity of taste and quality is not by luck but is awarded to our restaurant for quality that is fact. Insuring this quality, we maintain a very limited menu that specializes in only a very few items. Our focus is in serving the very best of the best.

Dear Tahir B,

Thank you for your review and we do understand that even local Vietnamese can be mistaken on the authenticity of a Banh Mi as to how it is constructed or what it should taste like. As such, with your being a visitor to Vietnam, we truly understand you being mistaken on “Banh Mi Authenticity.”

Our reply and explanation is a little lengthy but we feel obliged to not only serve great tasting authentic food from our Classic Home Cooking Style Kitchen but whenever possible, we seek to educate and correct potential diner misconceptions. 

READ ON ONLY IF INTERESTED IN AUTHENTICITY

BANH MI HISTORY AND AUTHENTICITY: One first needs to understand that the word Banh Mi in Vietnamese only means “Bread.” Next, one needs to understand that the French Chefs settling in Saigon in the 19th Century were the original creators and introducers of this sandwich to Vietnam. As the original sandwich was constructed on a French Baguette with a spread of Pate and layered with high quality roasted meat (Pork, Beef or Chicken) and finished with local greens of Cilantro, Cucumber, Slivered Green Onions and Chili, this sandwich was then coined and in future referred to as a Banh Mi.

DINING STATUS AFFLUENCE: As a result of the high quality ingredients, the Banh Mi was an expensive and quality sandwich that was primarily consumed only by the affluent who had the means to afford a Banh Mi. The cost of the authentic Banh Mi resulted in the word “Banh Mi” becoming somewhat of a dining status symbol that was associated with affluence.

ATTEMPTED REPLICATION CREATING THE “KNOCK OFF”: As the term Banh Mi itself simply meant bread and any filling, street vendors quickly seeking to reach the masses created a lower quality sandwich but as the term Banh Mi could be applied to any bread with any filling, these street push cart vendors could accurately refer to their lower grade “Knock Offs” as a “Banh MI.” To make a cheaper product and save on construction cost the street vendor used a lower quality bread, a composite mystery meat type filling and layered the filling with a generous dose of pickled vegetables and chili sauce to create the flavor the sandwich lacked and to also mask unwanted tastes and odors.

This is the Banh Mi understanding that many a Vietnamese moving abroad as an immigrant was exposed to. As such, when settling in their newly selected homelands, they simply replicated and introduced the lower quality chili sauce, pickled vegetable sandwich. The only difference between a local Vietnamese street sandwich and those served in a developed economy such as Australia is the quality of the lunch meat. Authentic, no….but mistaken by many a diner that does not know the difference. 

Instilling and broadening the misconception: As street vendors quickly permeated the streets with their cheaper Banh Mi “Knock Offs” being positioned on every street corner, this Knock Off by sheer volume availed to the budgeting masses served to create and instill the misconception that a “Pickled Vegetable, Chili Sauce Sandwich” was an authentic Banh Mi, but…. It is not.

This would be like you walking down a street and trying a pizza or hamburger at a franchised fast food outlet and believing that soggy pizza crust or a ground beef wafer smothered in mayonnaise and mustard was authentic and quality. 

Yes, when dining with us, you actually were served an authentic Banh Mi. It is important to remember Banh Mi origin, ….the baguette is a French creation and so is the Pate. These two items are the foundation of the authentic Banh Mi…. the garnishing with local greens or cilantro, cucumber and sliced chilis rather than the European lettuce and tomato created the original and authentic Vietnamese Banh Mi.

Your review deserves a detailed reply.

For your edification: The word Banh Mi in Vietnamese simply means “Bread.” History documents that when the French introduced a baguette and pate with quality roasted meats to Saigon in the 19th Century, the Vietnamese having no specific word in their language for a sandwich, they simply coined the original word “Bread” or Banh Mi for the French sandwich. Subsequently the loose usage of the term Banh Mi allowed for any bread, with any filling to also be referred to as a Banh Mi. 

Yes… in actuality a peanut butter and jelly sandwich can accurately be referred to as a Banh Mi.

As such, street vendors can accurately express they sell Banh Mis but this does not mean that their Banh Mi replicates the authentic French Banh Mi of acclaim. 

Basically, the use of the term Banh Mi is akin to the English use of the word “Fruit.” The term fruit encompasses many varieties that include apples, oranges, bananas, mangos etc., etc., etc. As such, the Banh Mi that is sold on the street can accurately be referred to as a Banh Mi (bread sandwich), but this Banh Mi does not mean it replicates the original and authentic Banh Mi introduced by the French. 

Sandwiches can differ significantly i.e. The comparison between a Jam sandwich to a steak sandwich is incomparable.

As you appear to be interested in food authenticity, should you choose to become better informed on the Banh MI and its history/origin, we have included some background reading for you should you have the time or interest.

History of the Banh Mi
The Banh Mi (sandwich) was introduced to Vietnam by the 19th Century French colonials settled in Saigon. The origin of the Banh Mi baguette is French, the Pate is French and the roasted meat used in construction were of quality French oven roasting of the Era. The only difference between a Parisian sandwich to that of the Vietnamese Banh Mi was the garnishing that resulted in making a significant difference in both taste and texture to that of the European/Parisian sandwich. The Banh Mi was constructed with local Vietnamese greens (cucumber, coriander and chilies) that replaced the traditional lettuce and tomato of the European/French sandwich. In essence, the “Banh Mi” may possibly be the first reported case of culinary fusion, thereby creating the first quasi-French/ Vietnamese culinary experience.

My Banh Mi (MBM):
As a result of MBM quality, our Banh Mis cost a little more than a street stall sandwich but the difference in quality, taste and authenticity is significant. You will notice that we at MBM use real roasted meats compared to street stalls that use a composite quasi luncheon type meat. These substitute fillings are constructed from unknown animal parts that are ground, emulsified and in many cases is dyed for coloring before compression to resemble a “Look Alike” luncheon meat.

The quality of our ingredients and the slow Home Cooking methods result in our food tasting different to that of a Vietnamese street stall or many a restaurant. The difference is that we prepare our meals with authentic pricey spices. We use a slow cooking process that has been abandoned by most kitchens. The taste of our meals is difficult to duplicate as most kitchens will use less expensive seasoning substitutes and take less time, making it impossible to create true Vietnamese authenticity of taste.

“What is Street Food?”
“Street Food” is a cheaper attempt to replicate classic Vietnamese food using lower grade substitutes to cut costs (for sale on the street). As such, street food is not authentic in taste in comparison to the home cooked Vietnamese food MBM specializes in (this is why our authentic meals taste different).

Basically, Street Food was designed to allow those on a tight budget and relegated to eating on the street, a cheap option to fill their stomachs. To a novice palate, Street Food may visually appear as Vietnamese but in fact, does not replicate authentic Vietnamese food in either taste or quality. Ask any Vietnamese if “Street Food” resembles anything close to what their families will serve during the TET holidays. The answer is NO.

MBM is noted for unique quality. Rated by patrons, food publications and pan-Asian television food channels, as serving Vietnam’s #1 Banh Mi for both taste authenticity and quality. Dear dohbinator,

Thank you for your review and mention of our quality meals and friendly food service.

One thing we would like to mention is that we do not serve a modern interpretation of the Banh Mi but actually serve an original authentic Banh Mi as was introduced to 19th Century Saigon by the French. 
It is important to understand that the word Banh Mi in Vietnamese simply means bread and is a loose term used for sandwiches (any sandwich). As such, the term Banh Mi does not denote a specific type of sandwich or construction. 

Unfortunately, over the past century, street stalls responding to the demand for inexpensive meals for street dwellers on a tight budget created a lower quality bread sandwich. As these street stalls selling the lower grade Banh Mi permeated the streets, visitors as well as some locals mistakenly thought of this Banh Mi as an original and authentic Banh Mi as originally introduced to Vietnam by the French. 

This association error would be comparable to an individual dining at a franchised fast food hamburger, taco or pizza stand in the West and mistakenly thinking that their meal was of the quality and authenticity of the name it carries. 

We hope that our explanation on Banh Mis is helpful to your understanding of the Sandwich and we thank you for your review.

Dear 320sherin,

Thank you for your review and commenting that your Vegetarian Tofu Banh Mi “was really tasty.” Regarding your comment on pickled daikon, we prepare an authentic Banh Mi as originally introduced to 19th Century Saigon by the French. In the original French introduction of the Banh Mi, pickled vegetables were not a prevalent part of the original sandwich construction. 

The original Banh Mi focus was directed to allowing the taste of their fillings (costly meats of Pork, Chicken or Beef) to prevail. Post introduction of original Banh Mi, popularity skyrocketed among the affluent who could afford a quality sandwich. This in turn resulted in the Banh Mi becoming somewhat of a status symbol. 

Unfortunately, due to the cost of the quality ingredient used in the construction of the original Banh Mi, access to this sandwich by the majority of diners was eliminated. As the word Banh Mi in Vietnamese simply means “Bread” and translates to any bread with any filling, street vendors used this opportunity to re-interpret and invent a cheaper version Banh Mi. This required the use of lower quality ingredients in order to create a price point that was affordable to a street diner that was not concerned with quality but more about something to fill an empty stomach. 

As the cheaper fillings had no flavor, the heavy influence of pickled vegetables and chili sauce was introduced to the street version Banh Mi. This created flavor for the lower grade composite fillings used and also masked any unwanted odors.

We at My Banh Mi construct with quality ingredients allowing the diner to focus on the flavors of the filling rather than pickles and chili sauce. Our Banh Mi is constructed to mirror the original and authentic Banh Mi as introduced by the French. This being the case, the taste of your tofu filling should dominate the flavor of the sandwich rather than pickles. To achieve this special flavor and a texture, our tofu is marinated in annatto seed oil and grilled to provide greater flavor and texture. Our Tofu Banh Mi construction objective is in ensuring that the flavor and texture of the tofu is protected and is not lost or overpowered by pickled vegetables.

Thank you for dining with us and we hope to have the opportunity to serve you once again.

This is exactly what we serve at My Banh Mi. 

On the other hand, with the French introducing the sandwich to Saigon, street vendors seeking to create a cheap sandwich for the masses and budget oriented diner used a cheaper roll that they filled with compressed luncheon meat and added chili sauce with pickled vegetable to add flavor to their mystery luncheon meats and to mask potential unappetizing odors. This cheaper sandwich also can be accurately referred to as a Banh MI. Basically, the word Banh Mi in Vietnamese is simply a generic term used for any bread and filling. In comparison to a street push cart Banh Mi (mistaken by many as an authentic Banh Mi), we operate a full service restaurant (not a street push cart) and are famed for our resurrection and the serving of an authentic Banh Mi. Our Banh Mis have been constructed to exactingly replicate the taste and quality of the original Banh Mi introduced to 19th Century Saigon by the French. Unfortunately over time this Banh Mi was lost as a result of a combination of circumstances brought about in Vietnam by conflicts, economic turmoil, costs and the loss of availability of the quality ingredients required in the construction of an authentic Banh Mi. 

You will have noted that the Banh Mis we serve are crisp freshly warmed baguettes that are layered with slices of slow oven roasted meats, a quality Pate spread and finished with the freshest of greens. In comparison, our Banh Mi significantly differs to a street cart version Banh Mi that uses a lower quality bread filled with a “mystery meat” composite type filling that is heavily loaded with pickled vegetables and chili sauce to add flavor and/or mask unwanted odors. 

Basically, the street sandwich is a cheaper pickled vegetable, chili sauce sandwich. This version of the sandwich was created over the years to serve as an inexpensive snack for the masses to fill empty stomachs. This is not an authentic Banh Mi but it can definitely be referred to as a Banh Mi as it is a sandwich and has its place for budget oriented individuals who prefer the flavor of pickled vegetable, a composite meat and chili sauce. You may have also noted that our baguettes may appear small but in actuality they are more dense than the street sandwich and weigh significantly more than a street baguette that is filled with air. 

Worthy of note is that the specialty of our restaurant is in the serving of authentic, quality Vietnamese home cooked food rather than offering cheap meals of low quality. Kheng T
Dear happyvirgo,

Thank you for your review and appreciation for the taste and quality of our authentic Banh Mi.
 
As you have expressed you are a “conniseurs of street banh mi,” it is easy to understand why you would notice a difference between our authentic Banh Mi and that of the Street Cart version you have dined upon previously. 

As you have shown interest in Banh Mis, should you be interested, I have provided a detailed reply on Banh Mis and the “Whats and Whys regarding their authenticity. 
The term “Banh Mi” in Vietnamese simply means “Bread” and this term was originally coined to the baguette sandwich that was introduced to 19th Century Saigon by the French Culinary masters of the day. 

In the introduction of the Banh Mi to Saigon, quality cuts of roasted beef, chicken or pork were layered on a spread of Pate within a crisp freshly baked baguette. 
 
As the freshly roasted meats were expensive, the original Banh Mi was a very expensive sandwich and was dined upon only by the affluent, this resulted in the Banh Mi becoming a status symbol. As such, street vendors understanding the term “Banh Mi” could be applied to any bread coupled with any type of filling, they quickly worked to construct a cheaper version of the Banh Mi in order to access a mass market and the budget oriented diner. This is a very similar practice to that of the fast food franchisers in the west.

In order to service the budget market, street cart vendors seeking to cut costs of their baguettes and to create what appears as volume, many cart vendors used baguettes that were baked using Potassium bromate. This is a compound that is used to expand the dough and to make the finished product appear light and airy. Unfortunately, unbeknownst to many, Potassium bromate is banned in many countries as it is classified as a category 2B carcinogen (possibly carcinogenic to humans) and considered such by the International Agency for Research on Cancer (IARC).[5A] (What does this all mean, who knows as we are also advised that if white mice eat enough white bread they develop cancer too.) 

Also, as a real meat filling is expensive, the original meat fillings have been substituted with a combination of various ground animal parts that have been constructed to appear as a luncheon meat. The cart vendors have also added an abundance of pickled vegetables and chili sauce to provide some flavor and mask unwanted odors. 

You will note that our Banh Mi filling are a recognizable roasted meat or Tofu and is not smothered with pickled vegetables and chili sauce. Instead, we allow the full flavors of our quality roasted meats to ultimately prevail. As a result of our focus on quality, we are recognized as serving Vietnam’s #1 Banh Mi which is rated for both authenticity of taste and quality.

We trust our explanation on the history of Banh Mi authenticity is helpful to you in recognizing what should be sought in the identifying of an authentic Banh Mi. 

Again, thank you for your review and we hope to have the opportunity to serve you once again in future.

Dear EAHL,

Thank you for your comment on our restaurant’s cleanliness and hygiene practices. Our serving great tasting food is important to us but just as importantly is our serving clean hygienic meals that are free from harmful street bacteria and are tummy safe. 

BACKGROUND ON BANH MI AUTHENTICITY FOR READERS WHO MAY BE INTERESTED. 

Regarding taste and authenticity, we are rated as Vietnam’s #1 Banh Mi for both authenticity of taste and quality. It is important to understand that most visitors and even many locals are not aware of what the authentic Banh Mi should look like or taste like. History documents the Banh Mi being introduced to 19th Century Saigon by the French culinary masters of that day. It was the French who introduced the Baguette and the Pate to Vietnam and along with this introduction, they created the first and original Banh Mi of Vietnam.

As Vietnamese understand, the word Banh Mi does not describe a particular sandwich but the word basically means bread. As such, after the French introduced their original sandwich, the term Banh Mi was later loosely coined to mean any bread with any kind of filling. As such, a peanut butter and jelly sandwich is as much a Banh Mi as is a Tuna Fish sandwich. Both are accurately described as a Banh Mi.

The French, when introducing the Banh Mi to Vietnam, simply assembled a sandwich as they would have in France but differentiated the Banh Mi by garnishing the sandwich with local Vietnamese greens rather than the lettuce and tomato they would have used in France. As such, the original and authentic Banh Mi was a very high quality sandwich that was filled with quality oven roasted meats (pork, beef, chicken) and then garnished with cucumber, cilantro and slivered chili. As this Banh Mi was a quality sandwich with expensive ingredients, the Banh Mi became a status symbol that was only affordable to the affluent. 

With the term Banh Mi signifying affluence but meaning bread with any filling, street vendors, seeking to capitalize on the affluence of the term “Banh Mi,” created a cheap street version using lower quality bread, a cheaper pate and, as oven roasted meat was too expensive, the street vendors created a composite meat product of unknown animal parts that was ground and compressed to form a quasi type lunch meat. As these composite fillings had little taste and sometimes exuded unwanted odors, vendors quickly added pickled vegetables and chili sauce to add some type of flavor and to importantly mask any unwanted odors.

As the street vendors tailored their Banh Mi version to be cheap, it permeated the streets and resulted in many an individual mistaking the street version to be the authentic Banh Mi when it is actually an entirely different sandwich. The term Banh Mi is not like “Hamburger” that requires a ground beef patty or “Hot Dog” that requires a sausage; as such Banh Mi can mean anything with bread. For this reason, Banh Mis cannot be compared except for those that are constructed in the same way and usually from the same vendor. 

We at My Banh Mi, differ to others as we prepare and serve an authentic Banh Mi that replicates the construction and quality originally introduced to 19th Century Saigon by the French. Our Banh Mi does cost a little more than the street version but that is because we use the highest quality ingredients, just as was used by the original French Chefs responsible for the introduction of the Banh Mi to Vietnam.

Hopefully our recalling Banh Mi history for you will assist you in future to recognize an authentic Banh Mi and to differentiate the various versions of Banh Mis that have been introduced by Banh Mi vendors globally.

Street vendors do not comply with any governmental standards …. Including health requirements. For this reason, street vendors can leave foodstuff in open containers on the street that lack refrigeration and are exposed to all flying, crawling and airborne bacteria. For these reasons, they have avoided the paying of a VAT tax to the government.

You are also correct with there being a 5 percent service charge for our well trained English speaking wait staff. By the same token this service charge is significantly lower than the 15 percent charged or expected in most western or developed countries/economies.

Dear AHH381,
Thank you for your review expressing we serve a “good sandwich” and that our restaurant is “very clean and service was great.”
Regarding your comment comparing our “Sandwich” in comparison to what you believe a Banh Mi should be, it may be helpful to provide some background on both the translation of the word and the history of the term Banh Mi origin.
Firstly, the word “Banh Mi” in Vietnamese simply means “Bread.” During the 19th Century, the French Culinary Masters of the Day introduced to Saigon a roasted meat sandwich on a spread of Pate layered within a crisp baguette. This baguette sandwich is recognized as the original and authentic Banh Mi. Consequently, after this introduction, anything added to bread and eaten as a sandwich was commonly coined a Banh Mi. 
As a result of the quality of meat and the Pate, the sandwich was relatively expensive and affordable only by the affluent. This Banh Mi affluence persona and the fact that anything with bread could be coined a “Banh MI” afforded the opportunity to street vendors to introduce their own version of a cheaper, lower quality Banh Mi that would be affordable to a broader consumer market. To accomplish this lower price, quality was diminished with the use of cheaper bread that used chemicals in replacement of yeast to cut cost and resulted in a less dense bread filling. Also, for the filling, a cheaper composite meat product was created and introduced to replace specific meat that would be more expensive. As the meats and the bread had very little flavor, generous portions of pickled vegetables and chili sauce were added to provide flavor and mask unwanted odors. 
As such, there are many versions of Banh Mi (sandwich) just as there are significant differences between a roast beef, tuna fish or deviled egg sandwich; this difference also exists when using the sandwich term of Banh Mi as well.
For instance, to demonstrate the diversity in the use of the term Banh Mi, there is one Banh Mi that is quite common, that consists of a spread of peanut butter and condensed milk on a baguette. This, in Vietnam, is also accurately referred to as a Banh Mi. 
 This being the case, when comparing Banh Mis it is important to compare the “Pickled Vegetable, Chili Sauce” Banh Mi purchased from a street cart to others of the same construction. 
We, on the other hand, do not compete for space in the lower quality Banh Mi market where diners are focused on a lower price and a lower quality bread product that is larger and capable of consuming more space in their stomach. As the cheaper “Pickled Vegetable, Chili Sauce” Banh Mi are more common on the street, it is easy to understand how many can confuse this as being a Banh Mi benchmark. Not dissimilar to our planet being visited by extra-terrestials who walked into a fast food burger outlet and gained the impression that this was the benchmark for all earthling sandwiches. 
As opposed to others, we are being recognized for serving the #1 Banh Mi in Vietnam and awarded for our Authenticity, Taste and Quality Ingredients.

Your review demands a relatively long explanation to address the comments you have posted. For those who are interested, it also serves as an educational piece on Banh Mi history and what to expect.
Thank you for your review expressing our Banh Mi “was definitely the best I had in my four week Vietnam travels. Also, the fact remains that we construct an authentic Banh Mi as was originally introduced to Saigon in the 19th Century by the French Culinary Masters of the day.
In addressing your much appreciated review, please allow me to first express that the word “Banh Mi” in Vietnamese simply means bread. Further, when the French combined their baguette with a filling, the term Banh Mi was expanded to include any bread with any filling and resulted in rendering the word Banh Mi to be “Coined” as any type of bread with any kind of filling. 
This being the case, a tuna fish or peanut butter and jelly sandwich can both be accurately referred to as a Banh Mi. As such, if you had eaten a peanut butter and jelly sandwich for lunch and someone asked you what you had eaten, you could accurately express to them you had a Banh Mi for lunch.
For this reason, Banh Mis will depart significantly in flavor, taste, construction and quality from one another. The term of a Banh Mi significantly differs to the construction demands of a hamburger requiring a ground beef patty on a bun or a hot dog that demands a sausage of some type. There is no criterion for a Banh MI per se. 
 To clarify the street Banh Mi that you mention is priced at VND15,000, you should also be aware of how these Banh Mi versions came about. The original and authentic Banh Mi, introduced by the French, was a high quality sandwich constructed on a French Baguette. The baguette was layered with quality portions of oven roasted meats (beef, chicken or pork) that was placed on a spread of a quality Pate and finished with a garnish of fresh local greens that comprised, cilantro, slivered chilis, and cucumber. As a result of the quality of this sandwich, consumption of this item was limited to only the affluent who could afford to dine on this quality, which resulted in the Banh Mi becoming a status symbol.
As a result of the diner affluence and status aspect attached to the term “Banh Mi,” street vendors, seeking to reach a broad consumer market, commenced the construction of a lower quality bread and meat type product (in many cases a mystery type of composite meat product) in order to generate access to the broad consumer market. As the bread fillings were questionable and lacked flavor, most vendors applied a heavy garnish of pickled vegetables and chili sauce to provide flavor and mask unwanted tastes or odors.
We, on the other hand, construct an authentic Banh Mi that replicates the construction and quality as that of the original Banh Mi introduced to Saigon in the 19th Century. As such, upon your trying our Banh Mi you commented with “definitely the best I had in my four week Vietnam travels” and the reason for your dining experience is a result of the quality of ingredients we use. For instance, the beef we use is imported grass fed Australian Striploin or a New Zealand or American “USDA Choice” rated Ribeye cuts.

As we all know, there is no substitute for quality and quality does cost a little more. 
As such, it is only with our time consuming traditional home cooking methodology are we able to provide our loyal patrons the quality and authenticity of taste they demand and for which we are famed for. 
Regarding our cake, the reason for the quality of taste and price is related to the quality of imported chocolate we construct with. Our focus is directed to the diners of discerning taste who demand good value for money. As opposed to other restaurants or hotels that expound five start quality food, we actually provide five star quality but at moderate prices representing great value.

Dear Kevin H,
Thank you for your review and your mention that “Food was good as was the service”. We pride ourselves on our food hygiene, quality of taste and authenticity.
Regarding your comment on authenticity of flavor and taste, we understand it is difficult for visitors or even Vietnamese to be aware of Vietnamese culinary history and to understand what authentic flavors are, or how or where they originated. For instance your comment on our Banh Mi being possibly a “little bit too polished,” it is important for one to take into account as to how, who and where the original and authentic Banh Mi came about. Culinary history documents the original and authentic Banh Mi being introduced to 19th Century Saigon by the French. The authentic Banh Mi was a very polished quality sandwich and constructed on a French baguette and layered with high quality roasted meats (beef, chicken or pork). This sandwich differed to a sandwich constructed in France only by the greens used to dress the sandwich. Instead of the conventional western lettuce and tomato being used as in a sandwich constructed in France, the French chef in Vietnam replaced the western greens with local greens such as cilantro, slivered green onions, cucumber and created a very high quality sandwich never previously available in Vietnam. The end product was a high quality French/Vietnamese fusion culinary creation.
As a result of this quality and the inherent cost of the authentic Banh Mi’s ingredients, the original Banh Mi was exclusively dined upon only by the affluent resulting in the Banh Mi rapidly being recognized as a dining status symbol. Further edification on Vietnamese sandwich history is that the word Banh Mi, in Vietnamese, simply means bread and has commonly been coined to refer to any bread with a filling, (a jam sandwich can accurately be referred to as a Banh Mi). 
As such, street vendors, recognizing the word Banh Mi as being a status symbol and seeking a food product to market to the masses, created a degraded quality sandwich which they could advertise using the term “Banh Mi.” In many cases, as a cost cutting measure, vendors often use a mystery meat or composite meat substance to replace the quality roasted meat demanded by the authentic and original Banh Mi. You will probably notice that in these degrade quality Banh Mi versions, the Banh Mis will often be laden with an abundance of pickled vegetable and chili sauce. This addition was added by vendors to provide flavor to their sandwich and to also mask unwanted flavors.
Logically speaking, can you imagine the originating French Chefs roasting a quality piece of beef and then masking the flavor with pickled vegetables and a chili sauce?? Hopefully, we have provided some answers to your mention of authenticity.
Regarding flavor and taste, this, of course, is a very personal matter and I am sure many a diner likes pickled vegetables and chili sauce to accent their meats or sandwich fillings. No different to one’s personal taste desiring ketchup or mustard on your hamburger or French fries. 
We are very cognizant that quality and the freshness of our food is paramount, as such our greens are hand-picked several times a day and our baguettes are served crisped and warmed fresh from our ovens. Our Banh Mis have been constructed to exactingly replicate the high quality polished Banh Mis as they were originally introduced. 
We hope our explanation of Banh Mi history and origin assist you in understanding more about the Banh Mi’s history and authenticity of taste.
Thank you so much for your review and we hope to have the opportunity to serve you once again in future and to again share with you our very authentic home cooked Vietnamese food.

Dear Amy S,
Thank you for your review comment on the good service we provide. With regard to flavor of the rolls, please note that Banh Mi in Vietnamese denotes bread and is generically used when referring to any sandwich. This being the case, there is no construction standard required when using the term Banh Mi. It is not similar to a hamburger or a hot dog term that requires a ground beef patty or a sausage, as such Banh Mi can be anything that uses bread in making a sandwich.
Our taste difference compared with the Banh Mi of most others is that we construct an authentic Banh Mi that mirrors the taste and quality of the original Banh Mi introduced to 19th Century Saigon by the French. This calls for the construction of this French sandwich to contain layers of quality roasted meat layered upon a spread of pate in a fresh crisp French baguette. As this sandwich was expensive, street vendors attempted to mimic this sandwich using lower grade of composite mystery meats and to provide flavor via a large dose of pickled vegetables.
Vietnamese immigrants that migrated to foreign countries did not replicate the authentic Banh Mi as it was originally constructed but instead replicated the less expensive street version which in most cases, is a night and day difference in taste.
We hope this explanation helps you to understand the difference in taste between our Banh Mi and what many others may serve. Our focus in our Banh Mi construction is authenticity of taste and the use of the finest ingredients available. As quality to us is paramount, if you had our Beef Banh Mi, it would have been filled with slices of a slow oven roasted Australian Strip Loin of beef. We do understand that taste is a matter of personal preference and if you have become accustomed to pickled vegetables on your Banh Mi, we totally understand.

Dear Rohan T,
Thank you for making time to craft and post a review. As you have taken the time to mention our Banh Mi, I would like to be helpful to you and provide you with a little background understanding on the Banh Mi and what a “Real Authentic” Banh Mi should taste like. Very briefly, the word Banh Mi in Vietnamese simply means bread. On a broader basis the Vietnamese have coined this term to generically refer to a sandwich…. “Any Sandwich.” As such, a tuna fish or a peanut butter and jelly sandwich can both be correctly referred to as a Banh Mi. 
As such, to document authenticity, one must recall that the original and authentic Banh Mi was introduced to 19th Century Saigon by the French culinary masters of the day. At that time the French understandably constructed their sandwich on a French baguette, introduced a spread of pate and then layered slices of a high quality roasted meat (beef, pork or chicken) as the filling. Rather than the insertion of lettuce and tomato as may have been used back in France, the sandwich was finished with local greens in order to accent their sandwich with local Vietnamese flavors. 
Quite simply, as a result of the quality of the ingredients very few, except the affluent, could afford this sandwich and as such, the Banh Mi became somewhat of a status symbol. Responding to the fact that anything in bread could be referred to as a Banh Mi, local street vendors, in order to reach a mass market, reproduced a lower quality sandwich with many using an inexpensive composite mystery meat to cut cost. As a result of the lower priced ingredients, used by the street push-cart merchants, the quality of taste of their Banh Mi suffered significantly. In addition, as there is no refrigeration and also to augment taste, the street vendors introduced large doses of pickled vegetables and bottled chili sauce to provide some flavor and to mask unwanted tastes.
As in life I am sure you can appreciate, there is no substitute for quality and quality costs more. For this reason you will not find pickled vegetables or bottled chili sauce on our Banh Mi to provide flavor. We do not hide or mask the flavors of our meats as they are slow oven roasted to insure succulence and to lock in the great inherent flavors of the quality cuts of meat we use. Just as you would not bury a good steak under a pile of pickled vegetables and douse this with bottled chili sauce, we use none of these flavor influences to overwhelm the taste quality of our meat and the crisped warm baguette that our Banh Mis are constructed with. As such, our Banh Mis are constructed to render the authenticity in taste and texture to that of the original Banh Mi introduced to 19th Century Saigon by the French.
We understand that taste is a very personal matter and that you may prefer or have become used to the taste of pickles and chili sauce on your Banh Mi. As such, we totally understand your comments on what you believe as authentic in taste. As you will note a large portion of our patronage comprises local, discerning Vietnamese residents (please view our photo library on the TA site), as such, we do not consider hygiene, quality of ingredients and providing a comfortable dining ambience as “Touristy.”

The reason for our difference in taste and quality is that we serve an authentic Banh Mi that exactly replicates the Banh Mi sandwich that the French Chefs originally introduced to 19th Century Saigon. The majority of diners today are totally unaware that the original Banh Mi was a sandwich that demanded quality roasted meat and pate to be layered on a crisp baguette. As the original Banh Mi was an expensive item, it quickly became a status symbol and consumption of the Banh Mi was basically limited to only the affluent. 
The street vendor of past did what today’s fast food vendors do and they construct a cheaper version of a quality product to market to the masses. As the cost of real roasted meats was expensive, many substituted composite type mystery meats and smothered the filling with pickled vegetable to mask the flavorless fillings. GohH76
Dear Jessica2394,
In response to your review, it appears that you were obviously seeking a street push-cart version of a Banh Mi, as opposed to an authentic Banh Mi as we serve.
I believe if you understand the word Banh MI, in Vietnamese, it simply is used as the generic term for a sandwich… any sandwich. As I have mentioned to others, peanut butter and jelly sandwich can be correctly referred to as a Banh Mi. 
As for authenticity of taste, the authentic Banh Mi is one that was introduced to19th Century Saigon by the French. This was and still is the original and authentic Banh Mi in flavor and texture. Basically, the French introduced a French Baguette sandwich that was filled with either oven roasted beef, chicken or pork that was layered on a spread of pate. At the time the French sandwich was introduced to Saigon, it was identical in every sense to a sandwich constructed in France. The only difference between the two was that the French sandwich constructed in France used European greens such as lettuce and tomato whereas the Colonial French replaced the European garnish with local Vietnamese greens such as cilantro, cucumber and in some cases chilis. This sandwich became what is known today as the authentic and original Banh Mi. The original Banh Mi was a sandwich that, due to the quality of the meats and preparation, was quite expensive. As such, the Banh Mi became somewhat of a status symbol with consumption limited to only the affluent. 
Because of the high cost of the quality items required by an authentic Banh MI, the street push-cart vendors, in order to meet a mass market, created a lower priced version of the sandwich using cheaper composite type meats and other lower quality substitutes. As the fillings did not contain the flavors of the oven roasted meats that the higher priced authentic Ban Mi possessed, the street vendor added heavy doses of pickled vegetables and fish sauce to provide flavor.
Vietnamese food is very delicate and prepared so as not to be overpowered with the flavors of fish sauce or pickled vegetables. Cooking preparation is designed to avoid allowing any one ingredient to mask all else.
As for our Banh Mi, we specialize in serving an authentic high quality Banh Mi that is constructed under the most demanding hygienic standards requiring the highest quality ingredients. We do believe that US$2.50 for our Traditional Banh Mi represents very good value for money when considering our hygiene practices, the quality of our Banh Mi and the air conditioned, table service seating. 
We trust that our explanation provides you a better understanding of what a truly authentic Banh Mi should taste like. Thank you for dining with us.

We understand that preference of taste is an individual matter, but I believe it important that we should take the time to explain to both you and your fellow TripAdvisor readers what an authentic Banh Mi should taste like. 
You mention that if diners are seeking to try a “westerner roll style baguette this place will suit you perfectly.” As such, I believe it important you should understand a little background on the origin of the Banh Mi. It is important to understand that it was the French in the 19th Century that produced and introduced the original Banh Mi to Saigon. This is the reason for the crisp baguette, pate and the roll being filled with layers of quality oven roasted beef, chicken or pork. 
Basically, the French took their Western sandwich and instead of finishing their sandwich with the traditional lettuce and tomato as garnish, they instead substituted the lettuce and tomato with Vietnamese cilantro, cucumber and other local greens to merely accent their sandwich. The local greens were primarily to only accent the filling but not to overpower the flavor of the roasted meat that their sandwich was filled with. 
This original French sandwich that was constructed with very high quality oven roasted meats, when complimented with the local Vietnamese greens, became the original Banh Mi. Further, as a result of the French sandwich construction quality and cost, the Banh Mi soon became a recognized status symbol and was primarily consumed by only the affluent Vietnamese who could afford this type of quality.
As “Banh Mi” in Vietnamese means “Bread” or categorically stand for a sandwich (any sandwich), the term Banh Mi does not denote the type of sandwich filling, construction, the bread or the taste. In fact, a “Peanut Butter and Jelly” sandwich can also be accurately referred to as a Banh Mi. 
As the authentic Banh Mi was an expensive item and as the term could be used for anything with bread, sidewalk push-cart vendors seeking to cut the cost of a Banh Mi to meet the mass market, constructed a sandwich with composite meats and gelatins that contained other mystery meat products. As the filling of the cheaper “Banh Mi” lacked the flavor of a quality roasted meat, the vendors masked their sandwiches with generous amounts of pickled vegetables to create some type of flavor.
As for our restaurant, we serve an authentic Banh Mi that exactingly replicates the quality and flavor of that introduced by the French to 19th Century Saigon.
Documenting and validating the authenticity and quality of our Banh Mi is the large number of loyal Vietnamese repeat diners that recognize the authenticity, hygiene, quality of ingredients and taste when dining on one of our Banh Mi.

More than the banh mi you may usually have whilst in Saigon
Mar 2016 • Friends
People visit a new country and they try "street food" or they eat something the locals would consider a "national" dish . Aside from the strong Viet coffee and the ubiquitous pho, one of the food items to taste when in Vietnam would be the seemingly simple banh mi - delicious, affordable, and they can be eaten without much fuss.

On our last night at Saigon, my friends and I were leaving the Saigon Central Post Office and crossed the road to come face to face with this restaurant and then... our stomachs growled. Yes, why not have some banh mi before we left for the airport?

We added two pasta dishes to our order of traditional banh mi (described in their menu as a freshly baked baguette with thin slices of their "House” slow-cooked oven roasted pork, and matched with any one of their six original homemade sauces) and France banh mi version (or what they call Banh Mi "Amour"). The latter was a freshly baked baguette stuffed with numerous slices of slow oven roasted sirloin strips served with smoked black pepper sauce.

We all agreed to share the banh mis we ordered so everybody could get a taste. We enjoyed both the creamily thick basil sauce and the pepper sauce we had opted for. 

The banh mis are more expensive here than what you may have tasted if you just got those ~VND 15.000 and above from street eateries. But let us face it, the banh mi here has also a higher quality set of ingredients.

Not to disparage the cheaper ones because I have personally tasted and can vouch for some delicious and freshly made banh mi fed to me by Vietnamese friends - and which I really enjoy, but the point is, the higher price means you expect better-tasting banh mi...and course you will also pay for the other intangible factors included in your servings. In this case, you do get your money's worth.

The service was made more superior by the charismatic presence Mr. Frank Chinn, who happens to be the loquacious and charming father of the owner - Chef Bobby Chinn. Now Mr. Frank I would say, would be the ace in Mr Bobby's sleeve - he would be the best resource that this restaurant has, aside from the good food they serve.

Mr Frank patiently answered our questions about the food we were planning to order (I bet we were the only table that time, wherein the whole group was debating quite loudly our choices hehehe!). He also made sure that not only taking our photograph with him was going to be a picture worthy of being posted on the internet, and last but not the least, he provided tips and guidance to the young, smiling employees who were attending to us at that time.

Ho Chi Minh has a lot going for it - not just the international cuisine available but also the local food. I definitely will have another banh mi here again, should I be in the vicinity, especially if I am in the mood for the more than the usual banh mi :-)

GohH76
Dear Fabian308,

Thank you for your review and we appreciate that taste is an individual matter of personal preferences. Regarding your comment that “the Banh Mie there was good, but it was hardly a Vietnamese taste.” It is important to understand that the Vietnamese word “Banh Mi” refers to bread or a sandwich in general and not a flavor or taste. 

As you are listed as being from Germany, we are sure you understand that there is a distinct difference between a “Butterbrot” and a “Fischbrötchen” or a “Mettbrötchen” sandwich. All are considered sandwiches, but they all are very different. As such, the same applies to the Banh Mi in Vietnam and if you have sampled a Banh Mi that differs from our authentic Banh Mi, we can understand that there may be a difference. 

Regarding your comment on authenticity of “more Western Banh Mie.” As edification, the Banh Mi was a French influenced sandwich introduced to Saigon in the 19th Century. The French constructed this sandwich on a crisp baguette, applied a spreading of Pate and generously layered the sandwich with very high quality roasted beef, chicken or pork. The Vietnamese influence to the authentic Banh Mi introduced by the French was their use of a small amount of local greens that were added to merely accent the roasted meat filling. 

As a result of the quality of the ingredients used in the French Banh Mi Sandwich, the original Banh Mi was considered expensive and only affordable to the affluent.

The Banh Mi quickly became a status symbol and permeated the country. This recognition of the Banh Mi status resulted in street vendors endeavoring to construct a cheaper version of the Banh Mi to serve the masses.
 
Street vendors attempting to create a cheaper Banh Mi sandwich forced their Banh Mi to be constructed with cheaper ingredients, such as; a soft roll, a lower quality Pate mixture and in many a case, the use of a lower cost composite meat type filling. You will notice that the street version Banh Mi sandwich is garnished with a liberal portion of pickles in order to provide flavor. 

We hope our explanation helps you to understand that the word Banh Mi in Vietnam is simply a generic term for all sandwiches.

Our restaurant specializes in serving an authentic quality Banh Mi as was originally introduced to Saigon. You are correct that our Banh Mi do cost slightly more (approximately US$ 2.00) than the cheaper Banh Mi versions sold from a street push-cart but this is due to the difference in our quality that calls for the use of slow roasted pork, chicken and beef (imported Australian and New Zealand) in the construction of our Banh Mi. 

If interested, please stop in so we can further explain our dedication to hygiene and “Quality over quantity.”

Thank you for your review.

Dear Jazonisatin,
Thank you for your review and writing where your palate very astutely distinguished the difference between our authentic Banh Mi and that of a sandwich purchased from a “street push-cart.” For possible fellow TripAdvisor review readers, to provide a little Banh Mi history and understanding, the word “Banh Mi” simply means “Bread” and is commonly coined in Vietnam when referring to a sandwich. As we all understand, sandwiches take many forms and taste, just as a “Tuna Fish Sandwich” is definitely different to that of a “Reuben” or a “Club,” the same applies to the Banh Mi.
As your palate already distinguished, the sandwich difference factor also applies to the Banh Mi sandwich in Vietnam. The original and authentic Banh Mi was introduced to 19th Century Saigon via a French/Vietnamese culinary collaboration. The original and authentic Banh Mi called for a fresh crisp baguette to be layered with high quality roasted meat (Pork, Chicken or Beef), with a spread of quality Pate and then garnished with a small amount of local greens. The original Banh Mi was a high-end sandwich that, as a result of the demanding quality of the ingredients, was relatively expensive and only dined upon by the affluent. As such, the original Banh Mi quickly became a recognized status symbol. 
As street vendors sought to create a Banh Mi product that was lower in price and affordable to the mass market, many a street vendor significantly downgraded the ingredients of their Banh Mi Sandwich by constructing their Banh Mi with composite type meats on a lower priced soggy roll, lower quality Pate and smothering their sandwich with pickled vegetables to add flavor to their “Mystery meat” and Pate.
As such, the Authentic Banh Mi we prepare and serve is significantly different to the sandwich purchased from the street push-cart. Dear TO_SG5,

Thank you for your review and appreciate your comments recognizing that our “restaurant is clean, in a great locale, has fresh, tasty bread.”

We have also noted your comment of “it did not live up in authenticity,” unfortunately many individuals in recent years are mistaken as to what “is” and “is not authentic” with regards to the Vietnamese Banh Mi. Please recall that the Banh Mi was introduced in the 19th Century to Saigon by a combination French/Vietnamese culinary collaboration. At the time of introduction, the authentic Banh Mi was a high quality sandwich that contained a spread of quality Pate on a crisp baguette and layered with oven roasted meats (chicken, beef or pork) and finished with a garnish of local greens. 

As a result of the quality of ingredients required, the original and “Authentic” Banh Mi was an expensive sandwich that quickly became a status symbol that was only affordable by the affluent. As a result of the Banh Mi’s wildfire popularity and the associated social economic status, many Vietnamese street vendors degraded the sandwich by lowering the quality with cheaper ingredients in order to service the mass market. 

As such, lower quality “Knock offs” of the original Banh Mi have unfortunately been mistaken by many to consider this lower grade version of the Banh Mi as the benchmark. 

Also, your comment of “There is very little inside the sandwich in terms of meats and veg” is a result of the flavor of the high quality roasted meats (our beef is an imported Striploin from Australia and Rib Eye from New Zealand) used in our Banh Mis that do not require a massive stuffing in order to create nutritional value and great flavor. 

We believe the Banh Mi you refer to are constructed with look-alike composite type meat products and as such, they do require an insertion of a massive amount of pickled vegetables in order to give their Banh Mi flavor.

As we have noted, you state yourself as being from Singapore, as such, we are sure that you appreciate that in life you get only what you pay for. 

As we will only serve to our patrons an authentic Banh Mi, this requires that we observe demanding hygienic storage and preparation, quality of meat, bread and the ancillary construction items being used in our Banh Mi construction. As such, we firmly believe that the $2.50 for our Traditional Banh Mi represents great value for money. 

We believe that in comparison, if you could find a Banh Mi of similar quality in Singapore, it would probably cost you at least 3 times the reasonable price that we charge (I believe there is a place on Orchard Road). We thank you for your review comments and trust our explanation above better enlightens you as to the origin of the Banh Mi and what you should look for and expect if you are truly seeking an authentic Banh Mi.
